_comment: Step 10 -- Rails 7.2 to Rails 8.0, on the interpreter step 08 installed.
Six gates, total weight 17, and they are two subjects and not six.  Three
are the release: the framework that boots, the declaration the application
makes, and the three settings that declaration turns on.  Three are one
gem: the one dependency in this Gemfile that cannot come to 8.0, the fork
that replaces it, and the call site the swap leaves behind.
The pin itself is easy and the profile says so with its weights.  Measured
in build/probe10/findings.md: `bundle lock --conservative --update rails`
from step 09's lockfile moves the thirteen framework gems to 8.0.5.1, adds
`uri` and drops `cgi`, 149 gems either side, and on the pin alone the tree
installs, boots development, test and production, and runs its 504 examples
green.  Nothing is capped, floored or held.  So, as at step 09, the
substance is what the pin does NOT do by itself.
-- the release --
`load_defaults 8.0` is three assignments (railties-8.0.5.1
configuration.rb:337-347) and this is the first rung on the ladder where
every one of them is live on this box: `to_time` keeps the receiver's zone
instead of its offset, an ETag takes precedence over `Last-Modified` when a
conditional request sends both, and `Regexp.timeout` is one second --
readable only because the interpreter is 3.2.  One of the three the release
forces: Active Support deprecates every value of `to_time_preserves_timezone`
but `:zone` and attributes the notice to this application's own
`config/environment.rb`, so a tree that takes 8.0 and declines its defaults
fails the inherited `boot_quiet` and `own_deprecations` guards and scores no
gates at all.  That is the release holding the door, not this profile.
-- the gem --
`annotate`'s last release caps `activerecord < 8.0`.  What makes that worth
three gates is what bundler does with the cap: asked conservatively for
Rails 8 it reports no conflict and resolves `annotate 2.6.5`, from June
2014, whose only constraint is `activerecord >= 2.3.0`.  The tree installs,
boots, passes the suite, and still annotates.  Every instrument this task
had before this step calls that a pass.
And the correct swap has a trap in it that the same instruments also miss.
`lib/tasks/auto_annotate_models.rake` -- 2014's installer output, twenty-one
options and `Annotate.load_tasks` -- names a constant `annotaterb` does not
define.  Rake loads every file under `lib/tasks/` before it runs anything, so
the file left in place beside the fork is not a broken annotate task: it is a
broken `rake`, `db:migrate` and `assets:precompile` included, in development
only, because line 4 of that file is `if Rails.env.development?`.  Boot is
green.  All three environments are green.  The 504 examples are green.
So the step measures it twice and on purpose: `annotate_legacy_api_gone`
counts the call sites statically, and the `rake_tasks_load` guard runs
`RAILS_ENV=development bundle exec rake -T` and reads its exit status.  The
count can say which line; the exit status can say that it matters.  The
guard is a guard and not a seventh gate because the tree this step is handed
already passes it -- 50 tasks, exit 0, on Rails 7.2 with annotate 3.2.0 --
and design rule 4 / notes section 7.18: a property the handed-on tree already
has is a floor, not a point.
-- what is NOT gated here --
`.annotaterb.yml` is not gated, although the reference solution writes it.
The generator's output is the fork's own defaults dumped to a file, and the
defaults that matter here -- the five `position_*` settings at `before`,
`show_indexes` true, `model_dir` `app/models` -- are already what the 2014
file set them to (build/probe10/findings.md section 10, and the fork's own
`annotate_rb/options.rb` DEFAULTS).  A tree with no
config file annotates identically to one with the generated file, so a gate
on its presence would be a point for having run a generator.  What it would
have protected is covered: the annotations themselves are in the seven model
files, and `tree_intact` and the behaviour cases read those files.
The Solid trio (Solid Queue, Solid Cache, Solid Cable) and Kamal are not
gated and are not asked for.  They are what `rails new` writes on 8.0, not
what `load_defaults 8.0` turns on: this application has no Active Job
backend to move, no cache store configured beyond the default, no cable, and
no deploy in the repository (build/probe10/findings.md section 9).  Adding
them would be new infrastructure, which is not a migration.
-- the ladder --
Step 09's six other gates are guards here, which is the rule: what a rung
earns, the rung above stands on.  Two inherited checks are narrowed, both
because 8.0 withdrew a setting they were asserting, both with `absent_keys`
over the survivors, and both argued in the guard's own description:
`framework_defaults` stops asserting `to_time_preserves_timezone` (5.0 said
`true`, 8.0 says `:zone`, and the new value is gated on this page instead),
and `defaults_7_2_adopted` stops asserting
`aj_enqueue_after_transaction_commit` (railties 8.0's own `when "7.2"`
branch no longer assigns it; the option was withdrawn).  Neither narrowing
is a concession to a tree -- no tree on Rails 8 can satisfy either, and a
failing guard zeroes 0.55 of the reward.  Measured both ways in
build/probe10/out/bp-r5.json and written up in findings.md section 11.
Behaviour is 0.45 and the gates family 0.55, as on every step.  Guards carry
no weight and one failing guard zeroes the gates family.

gates.desc: Rails 8.0 is the framework that boots -- not 7.2, and not 8.1.  The reading is the version of the `rails` the booted application loaded, taken from the running process rather than from the Gemfile, so a lockfile that says one thing and a tree that loads another is visible.  As at step 09 the Gemfile change is a single line and nothing is capped, floored or held: `bundle lock --conservative --update rails` from the 7.2 lockfile moves the framework's own thirteen gems, adds `uri 1.1.1` and drops `cgi 0.5.2` -- default gems the 8.0 dependency graph names and stops naming -- and on the pin alone the tree installs, boots all three environments and runs its 504 examples green (build/probe10/findings.md sections 1-7).  That is why the weight is 2 rather than the 3 the harder pins on this ladder carry.  The INTERPRETER does not move here and there is no ruby gate on this page: railties 8.0.5.1 raises `required_ruby_version` to 3.2.0 and the tree has been on 3.2.11 since step 08, so a gate on the interpreter would be a point for having changed nothing -- it is guarded below instead, and the release that does move it is step 12.  What the pin does NOT do by itself is the rest of this page: the defaults below, and the one gem in this Gemfile that cannot come to 8.0 with it

and `config.load_defaults 8.0` is the declaration it boots with, read off the application's own `loaded_config_version` rather than off the source line, so a tree that writes the line into a file the framework never evaluates does not pass it.  One line, and the gate below is what it turns on

and the three 8.0 settings are actually at their 8.0 values.  The reading is the list of the ones that are not, so a partial adoption names itself; it is 3 of 3 missing on the tree this step is handed and 0 of 3 on the migrated one (measured, build/probe10/out/readers-r1.json and bp-r5.json).  Three, and all three counted, which is why this is the heaviest gate on the page and why it is 4 where step 09's equivalent was 3: railties 8.0.5.1's `when "8.0"` branch (configuration.rb:337-347) makes exactly three assignments and every one of them is readable on THIS application, on THIS image -- the first rung on this ladder where that is true.  Each is read where the framework really consults it.  `as_to_time_preserves_timezone` off `ActiveSupport` and through `.to_s`, because the adopted value is the symbol `:zone` and the value it replaces is `true`; it is also the one setting of the three this release FORCES, because Active Support's writer deprecates anything but `:zone` and attributes the notice to this application's own `config/environment.rb`, where `Rails.application.initialize!` runs -- so a tree that takes 8.0 and declines this default fails the inherited `boot_quiet` and `own_deprecations` guards and scores no gates at all.  Nothing in this application calls `to_time`: the only conversion in app/, lib/, config/ or db/ is `answer.created_at.to_date` in the weekly-activity mailer, and `to_date` is unaffected, so the flip changes no recorded byte -- which is why it is gated as a configuration reading and not chased into behaviour.  `ad_strict_freshness` off `ActionDispatch::Http::Cache::Request`, the class the railtie assigns it to, and not off `config.action_dispatch`: that is where a tree which declared 8.0 and then assigned `false` back is caught.  It is a declaration on this application and the instruction says so rather than claiming a behaviour change -- the flag is consulted inside `ActionDispatch::Http::Cache::Request#fresh?` (conditional_get.rb:154,238) whose only callers are `fresh_when` and `stale?`, and this application writes neither.  `regexp_timeout` off `Regexp.timeout`, a process-global of the interpreter rather than a framework setting, which reads back as the Float `1.0` because railties writes `Regexp.timeout ||= 1`.  It is readable here for a reason worth naming: `Regexp.timeout` exists from Ruby 3.2, which is the interpreter step 08 installed, so 8.0's third default is live on this box rather than silently skipped

and the `annotate` gem is not in the resolved bundle.  The reading is the lockfile's own spec list, so this is a fact about what would install and not about what the Gemfile asks for.  It is a gate on its own -- separate from the gem that replaces it -- because of what bundler does when it is left in.  `annotate`'s last release is 3.2.0 and its gemspec caps `activerecord < 8.0`, and asked conservatively for Rails 8 bundler DOES NOT REPORT A CONFLICT: it resolves `annotate 2.6.5`, published 2014-06-16, whose only constraint is `activerecord >= 2.3.0`.  The tree then installs, boots, passes all 504 examples and still annotates (measured, build/probe10/findings.md section 10) -- a ten-year silent downgrade that every other instrument on this page reports as success.  That is the shape this gate exists for: the failure that looks like a pass.  The weight is 1, the lowest on this page, and deliberately so: deleting a line is the easy half and it is also what the WRONG answer to this step does.  A tree that read `annotate` being capped as permission to drop the tool collects this point and then stops, and one point of the eight on this dependency is what that is worth; the gate below is where the other half of the swap is scored, and `model_annotations` among the guards is what makes taking the comments down with the gem fatal rather than cheap

and the maintained fork is in its place, at a release of the 4.x line or above.  `annotaterb` is the same tool under a new name -- same schema block, same `before` positions, same `db:migrate` hook -- and it is the one replacement that keeps the seven models' existing annotations byte-identical, which is what makes it a migration of this dependency rather than the removal of a feature.  The floor is `4.0.0` and not the exact release the reference solution locks, because the requirement is the line and not the patch: 4.x is the series that supports Rails 8, and a candidate who resolves a later 4.x has done the same work.  The reading is the lockfile's resolved version, as for the gate above; `version_at_least` compares it as a version and not as a string, so 4.10 is above 4.9.  Five of the eight points on this dependency are here, which is the arithmetic of the sentence above: the step is a SWAP, and the only reading on this page that a tree which merely deleted the gem cannot produce is the fork's presence.  Deletion still collects `annotate_gem_gone` and `annotate_legacy_api_gone` -- removing the Gemfile line and the rake file it configured -- so those two are worth 3 of 8 together and this one is worth 5 on its own, and the step cannot be half-passed by subtraction

and no call to the old gem's API is left in the tree.  The reading counts `set_defaults` and `load_tasks` written on the receiver `Annotate`, anywhere under the repository: 2 on the tree this step is handed -- both in `lib/tasks/auto_annotate_models.rake`, the file the 2014 installer wrote -- and 0 on the migrated one.  This is the gate the step is really about.  `annotaterb` defines `AnnotateRb`, not `Annotate`, and rake loads every file under `lib/tasks/` before it runs anything, so that file left in place is `NameError: uninitialized constant Annotate` raised while the task tree is being built -- `rake -T`, `rake db:migrate` and `rake assets:precompile` all gone, in development, which is where the file's own `if Rails.env.development?` puts it.  Boot stays green, all three environments stay green, the suite stays green: without this gate and the `rake_tasks_load` guard beside it, the half-done swap is indistinguishable from the finished one.  It is counted statically here and proved at runtime there, and the two are deliberately not the same instrument -- a count can say which line, and an exit status can say that it matters.  What the reference solution does is retire the file for `lib/tasks/annotate_rb.rake` and `.annotaterb.yml`, which is what `rails g annotate_rb:install` writes; the instruction requires the old API gone and the task tree loading, and does not require that spelling.  The weight is 2 rather than the 3 its prose would suggest because the realistic version of this mistake is already priced twice over: `rake_tasks_load` among the guards fails on exactly the tree this gate fails on, and a failing guard takes the whole gates family to zero.  Paying 3 here as well would count one mistake three times and leave the gem's replacement -- the part a candidate can only get by doing the work -- scored below it

guards.desc: the application boots in RAILS_ENV=production -- carried forward from step 02, as a guard rather than a gate because the tree this step is handed already does it
and in the `development` and `test` environments too, each in a process of its own
and with eager loading on, every file under the eager-load paths loading without raising
and every constant the application keeps outside `app/` is still defined once a production process has finished eager loading
the models still descend from `ApplicationRecord`
and none of them has been pointed back past it at `ActiveRecord::Base`
every migration still declares the schema version it was written against

and every one of the 43 migrations the repository shipped still declares 4.2, the release it was written against.  This is step 02's reading restored, and it replaces step 06's `migrations_still_4_2`, which counted misversioned migrations across the whole of `db/migrate/` and from step 07 on counts the one step 07's requirement added: that widening migration declares `ActiveRecord::Migration[7.0]`, because that is the release it was written against, which is the same rule that keeps the other 43 at `[4.2]`.  This step adds no migration of its own, and the inherited guard would still fail on step 07's.  Measured: on the step 07 golden `scan.counts.misversioned_migration` is 1 and the inherited guard fails, which would zero the whole gates family over a file the step asked for (build/probe07/out7/scan.json).  The shipped-restricted histogram is not a weaker reading -- it is the one that actually catches restamping, because a count over the whole directory is satisfied by dropping 43 dummy `[4.2]` classes beside the restamped originals

and the one association this application creates before its parent is known still says so on the association itself -- `Call#location` is written when the call arrives and its location is not known until the caller keys a location code. Step 02 scored this; here it is a guard, because the tree this step is handed already has it and a gate it passes for free would only raise the floor. It is carried forward at all because the gate above reads the application-wide default and nothing else: a tree that switched the default off would fail that gate, but a tree that left it on and marked every association optional would pass it, and this is the reading that notices

and no other association was marked optional to get there -- `optional: true` on every `belongs_to` in the tree leaves the application-wide default switched on, passes both readings above, and gives up exactly the constraint the default was switched on for. The repository has six `belongs_to` and one of them is the create-before-parent case, so the count of optional ones is at most that one
`belongs_to` associations are still required by default

and four of the five 5.0 framework defaults step 02 adopted are all still at their adopted values -- the reading is the list of the ones that are not, so the evidence names them.  Four and not five, and this is the rung where that changed: `to_time_preserves_timezone` is left out, because `load_defaults 8.0` assigns it `:zone` where 5.0 assigned it `true`, and `bootprobe.rb#adoption` compares against the 5.0 value.  That is not a tree that stopped adopting a default; it is the release moving one, and it is the one 8.0 setting this application cannot decline -- Active Support deprecates every other value of it, attributed to this application's own `config/environment.rb`, so a tree that held `true` here would fail `boot_quiet` instead.  Measured on the step-10 golden, build/probe10/out/bp-r5.json: `not_adopted` is exactly `["to_time_preserves_timezone"]` and the other four are adopted.  `absent_keys` over the four survivors names the tolerated one by leaving it out, which is the shape steps 08 and 09 chose for `defaults_6_1_adopted`, `defaults_7_0_adopted` and `defaults_7_1_adopted` and for the same reason: editing `wanted` in bootprobe.rb would move the reading under every step below this one, and the reading is honest -- it is the profile's job to say which of the five a given rung holds the tree to.  The value itself is gated on this page, at its 8.0 value, by `defaults_8_0_adopted`

driving the application raises no deprecation warning from its own code -- the budget step 02 set, now against 8.0's list rather than 7.2's. This is also the only reading of a *production* boot: the collector is installed before `config/environment.rb` is required, so a deprecation the application raises while production boots is counted here rather than by `boot_quiet`, which boots development and test. Warnings raised from inside a third-party gem's own source are out of scope; anything the application itself triggers, including from its own configuration, is in scope

and running the spec suite raises none from a file under spec/ -- taken by a collector prepended to `ActiveSupport::Deprecation` inside the suite's own process, so silencing the warnings does not remove them from it
and booting the named environments raises none from a file under `config/environments/`
the application's own spec suite runs to completion against the tree as handed on, and every example in it passes
and it still makes substantially every expectation it was handed: at least 495 examples
no comment in the source directs a tool to ignore a finding (rubocop:disable, brakeman:ignore, :nocov: and the rest) -- a tree that silenced the checks is not measured by them

every Ruby and ERB file in the tree parses under this step's interpreter -- a file the scanner cannot read is a file none of the source gates can see, so their counts would be lower bounds reported as answers

every file the repository shipped under spec/ is still there (77 of them, listed in pristine.json) -- deleting the application's own tests is not a way to have no findings in them. One fewer than step 04's 78, and inherited: `spec/support/factory_girl.rb` came off the list at step 05's factory_bot rename and stays off. This step drops no further path, so the list it is checked against is step 05's unchanged
every spec file the repository shipped still declares at least one example -- keeping the path and emptying the file is not a way to have no findings in it

the application is still there: every file the repository shipped under app/models, app/controllers, app/helpers, lib and db/migrate is still at its path (97 of them, listed in pristine.json) -- the migration removes what the framework removed, not the application's own code.  One fewer than at step 09, and it is this step's own doing: the manifest drops `lib/tasks/auto_annotate_models.rake`, the file that configured the gem Rails 8 leaves behind, because removing or replacing it is the work rather than damage to the tree

the shipped spec files still contain at least 220 distinct assertion lines -- the suite handed on to this step has 309, while a suite whose examples have been replaced by a tautology has one; keeping the paths, the declarations and the example count while asserting nothing is not a way to pass the suite

no spec file the repository shipped has been left declaring examples that assert nothing. The count above is a floor over the union of the tree's distinct assertion lines, and a union has a shape it cannot see: one file carrying every surviving assertion and fifty carrying none reaches the same number as fifty files that each kept their own. Every shipped spec file that is still present and still declares an example has at least one assertion line of its own

and every file the suite ships that had content of its own still has some -- the 27 shipped factories, fixtures, helpers and Teaspoon files are judged by existence alone by the three guards above, and `> spec/factories.rb` keeps the path, keeps the file count and removes every object the suite builds on. The reading is the shipped test files that had a non-blank, non-comment line in the baseline and have none now

the tree hands on config/database.yml.example and does not hand on config/database.yml -- the instruction says the configuration is produced from the example, and a tree that ships its own database.yml is scored against a database configuration the recording never used

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) the hand-written new-framework-defaults initializer is gone -- 5.1 introduces `config.load_defaults`, which is the framework's own replacement for that file, and one of the seven assignments the file carries (`ActiveSupport.halt_callback_chains_on_return_false =`) is itself deprecated on 5.1, so keeping it is a deprecation raised from the application's own configuration. The reading is the list of files under `config/initializers` whose NAME is the generated one (`new_framework_defaults*`); the file's contents are followed separately by the gate below, which is the reading a rename has to get past

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) and its contents have not simply moved somewhere else: none of the seven switches that file lists is assigned by hand anywhere in the tree. `config.load_defaults 5.1` is a declaration of the whole set at once, so a tree that declares it and also keeps `...active_record.belongs_to_required_by_default = true` in an initializer under some other name has kept the file rather than adopted the defaults -- and one of the seven assignments is deprecated on 5.1 wherever it is written. The list is that file's seven and no others: `assets.unknown_asset_fallback` is a switch 5.1 introduces and the 5.0 file never listed, so writing it by hand moves nothing out of that file and is not read here -- whether the fallback is actually off is the pair of runtime gates below. The reading is an assignment in the parsed source and not a mention, so the comment in `config/application.rb` that names the switches the declaration covers is not a finding

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) the asset pipeline no longer falls back to the public folder for a name it does not know, AND this application's own audio-URL helper still answers the public path for one, without raising and without warning. Every question this application plays over the phone is reached through `VoiceFeedbackHelper#voice_file_path`, whose argument is a question's short name and has never been a pipeline asset, so the two halves have to be read together: with the fallback on, that call answers and (from 5.1) deprecates; with it off, the same call raises `Sprockets::Rails::Helper::AssetNotFound` unless the caller asks for the public path explicitly. The reading is one boot-time probe of the helper itself against a name that is deliberately not an asset, so a tree that satisfies the setting and leaves the helper raising is named here

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) and so does the other audio path, `TwilioSessionError#voice_file`, whose argument is the error's own message -- the same reading taken of the second call site, because the two are separate code and a tree can fix one and leave the other raising at the moment a call goes wrong

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) the form this application serves is built with `form_with`, the builder 5.1 introduces to unify `form_for` and `form_tag` -- at least one call survives in the tree, so the requirement cannot be met by removing the form

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) and no `form_for` is left anywhere, including in the partial nothing renders -- a `form_for` in a file the next step's author will read as live is the half of this change that the recording cannot see. The reading counts calls in compiled ERB as well as in Ruby, so a builder called from a template is counted the same as one called from a helper

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) and the key is not still lying around in the clear -- anywhere in the tree, under any name. `config/secrets.yml` is the file step 01 created, carrying the same 128-character key in development and test; the reading is every file in the tree that is either named `config/secrets.yml*` (other than the `.enc` and the `.key` that belong there) or mentions `secret_key_base` while also carrying a 64-character run of hex, so moving the old file to `config/secrets.yml.bak` or leaving a copy under `spec/` is named here rather than passed. It is a reading of the tree and not of the framework's own `config/secrets` path, because 5.1 widens that glob to `secrets.yml{,.enc}` and therefore answers `present` for a tree that has only the encrypted file

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) the application's mailer takes its subject through Action Mailer 5.1's parameterization -- `NotificationMailer.with(...)` and `params[...]` rather than positional arguments -- and every action the mailer class itself declares does. The reading is the arity of the actions whose owner is the mailer class, so a view helper that reaches `action_methods` through an `include` is not counted against it, and a tree that parameterizes one action and leaves the other positional is named here

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) and every caller moved with it: no `NotificationMailer.confirmation_email(...)` or `.weekly_activity(...)` is left in the tree. The runtime reading above is of the mailer class, and a tree can parameterize the class while leaving the two callers and the two specs passing their arguments positionally -- on 5.1 that raises nothing, the action simply receives no parameters and the mail goes out addressed to nobody. The reading is a call to one of the two action names on the mailer class in the parsed source

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) no validation is conditioned on a String to be evaluated in context -- 5.1 deprecates that at class-definition time, so this application deprecates three times before it serves anything. The reading asks each model's own `validators` for the `:if`/`:unless` options the framework holds, so a condition declared in a concern or through `send` is counted the same as one written in place

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) the database this application builds by loading its own `db/schema.rb` and the database its own migrations build from empty have the same tables, with the same primary keys, and those keys are still the 32-bit ones this application's tables have today -- on a framework whose own default for an unnamed key has become the 64-bit one. Both databases are built inside the scored run, the second after everything else has been measured, and the reading names the tables the two disagree about, the tables only one of them has, and separately any key whose width it does not recognise at all, which is a finding rather than a pass. The dump alone would not do: a tree that hand-edits `db/schema.rb` would then answer for migrations that build something else. The framework's own default is part of the conjunction because on a release that still defaults to the narrow key the two constructions agree for free, and a requirement the handed-on tree already meets measures nothing

Active Record cache keys carry a version rather than a timestamp (`load_defaults 5.2`), still true under 7.1.  Steps 02 to 06 guarded these four, `form_with_generates_ids` and `hash_digest_class` as one list -- `defaults_5_2.not_adopted` empty.  That list cannot be empty at this step and no tree can make it so: railties' own "5.2" branch sets `hash_digest_class` to `OpenSSL::Digest::SHA1` where 6.1's set `::Digest::SHA1`, and the later branches supersede it again with `OpenSSL::Digest::SHA256` -- which both the `defaults_7_0_adopted` guard below and the `defaults_7_1_adopted` gate hold this tree to.  Measured on this step's own golden: `defaults_5_2.not_adopted` is `["hash_digest_class"]` (build/probe08/out/bootprobe-r3.json).  An inherited guard that the step's own requirement makes unpassable would zero the whole gates family, so the list is guarded reading by reading and the one reading the later defaults supersede is dropped (`form_with_generates_ids` has had a guard of its own since step 03 and keeps it) -- the same rule that keeps the previous rung's `load_defaults` and framework-version readings out of this step's inherited list
